# Design Twitter

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Twitter / X • Threads • Bluesky • Mastodon` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The entire hard part of Twitter is the timeline, not the tweet: a celebrity with 100 million followers turns 'write one tweet' into a **fan-out** problem of enormous scale, and every real design decision here is about ==when that fan-out actually happens==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a simplified version of Twitter: users can post short text messages
("tweets"), follow other users, and see a home timeline showing recent
tweets from everyone they follow, in roughly reverse-chronological order.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the follower distribution like? Are there celebrity accounts with tens of millions of followers?
*Why it matters:* A uniform 'everyone has ~200 followers' system and a system with Justin Bieber-scale accounts need completely different timeline architectures. This single fact decides the entire **feed-generation strategy**.

#### Q: Does the timeline need to be perfectly real-time, or is a few seconds of staleness acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Perfect real-time ordering across a distributed system is expensive. A few seconds of ==eventual consistency== opens up much cheaper, much more scalable designs.

#### Q: Do we need to support search, retweets, likes, and media (images/video), or just the core post-and-follow-and-read loop?
*Why it matters:* Each of those is close to its own system design problem. Scoping them out lets the interview focus on the genuinely hard part: timeline generation at scale.

#### Q: Should the timeline be pure reverse-chronological, or does it need ranking/relevance scoring?
*Why it matters:* Chronological is a well-understood fan-out problem. Ranked feeds add a whole separate scoring/ML layer on top, which is a materially different (and harder) system.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can post a tweet (short text, optionally with media).
- A user can follow and unfollow other users.
- A user can view their home timeline: recent tweets from everyone they follow, newest first.
- A user can view another user's profile timeline: just that user's own tweets.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Reading a home timeline must be fast, well under a second, since it's the single most-loaded page in the entire product.**
- **The system must tolerate extreme skew in follower counts, from zero followers to tens of millions, without the celebrity accounts degrading the experience for everyone else.**
- **High availability for reads: a user should always be able to see some timeline, even if it's a few seconds stale, rather than see an error.**
- **Eventual consistency is acceptable: a followed user's new tweet can take a few seconds to appear in a follower's timeline.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 200 million daily active users
- Average user posts 1 tweet every 2 days; average user checks their timeline 5 times a day
- Average follower count is 200, but a small number of celebrity accounts have 50 million+ followers
- Each tweet is roughly 300 bytes of text plus metadata

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Tweets written per day:** 200,000,000 / 2 = 100 million tweets/day ≈ 1,160 writes/sec average, low compared to reads
- **Timeline reads per day:** 200,000,000 * 5 = 1 billion reads/day ≈ 11,600 reads/sec average, and far higher at peak hours
- **Fan-out writes for an average tweet:** 1 tweet * 200 average followers = 200 fan-out writes; totally fine to do per-tweet
- **Fan-out writes for a celebrity tweet:** 1 tweet * 50,000,000 followers = 50 million fan-out writes for a single post, which is the number that breaks a naive design

*Capacity Takeaway:* This is a **read-heavy system** overall (roughly 10:1 reads to writes), but the real danger isn't the average case, it's the ==extreme skew==: a single celebrity tweet can demand more fan-out work than the rest of the platform combined, which is why timeline generation strategy is the entire design problem.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A write path: a user posts a tweet, it's saved to the tweets store, then a
fan-out service asynchronously pushes that tweet's ID into the
pre-computed timeline_cache of every one of that user's followers. A read
path: a user opens their home timeline, the app server reads their
pre-computed timeline directly from the cache, already sorted, and merges
in any tweets from accounts too large to fan out on write (fetched live at
read time and blended in by timestamp). This **hybrid** is the entire design:
fan-out-on-write for normal accounts to make reads cheap, fan-out-on-read
for celebrity accounts to keep writes bounded.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Hybrid fan-out: write path and read path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    tweetdb[("Tweets Store")]:::db
    queue>"Fan-out Queue"]:::queue
    worker["Fan-out Workers"]:::server
    timelinecache["Timeline Cache"]:::cache
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"write tweet"| tweetdb
    app -.->|"enqueue fan-out"| queue
    queue -.-> worker
    worker -.->|"push to followers"| timelinecache
    app -->|"read timeline"| timelinecache
```

#### Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read

| Fan-out on write | Fan-out on read |
| :--- | :--- |
| Reads are cheap: just fetch a pre-built list | Writes are cheap and bounded, regardless of followers |
| Writes are expensive in proportion to follower count | Reads are expensive: must merge from every followee live |
| Breaks down badly for celebrity accounts | Used selectively, for celebrity accounts, in the hybrid model |

#### The hybrid model's routing decision, per tweet

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  tweet["New tweet posted"] --> check{"Does this account have a huge follower count?"}
  check -->|"no, typical account"| write["Fan-out on write: push to every follower's cached timeline now"]
  check -->|"yes, celebrity account"| skip["Skip the expensive push"]
  skip --> merge["Fan-out on read: merge into followers' timelines live, at read time"]
  write --> fast["Follower's read is a fast cache hit"]
  merge --> slower["Follower's read does a bit more work, but writes stayed cheap"]
```

#### Fan-out writes grow linearly with follower count

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/tweets` | Body: { text, media_url? }. Creates a new tweet from the authenticated user. |
| `POST` | `/api/users/{userId}/follow` | The authenticated user follows userId. |
| `GET` | `/api/timeline/home` | Returns the authenticated user's home timeline, paginated, newest first. |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/tweets` | Returns userId's own tweets, paginated, for their profile page. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `tweets`
- `tweet_id (unique, roughly time-sortable, e.g. Snowflake-style ID)`
- `author_id (indexed)`
- `text (short string)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* The single source of truth for tweet content, sharded by author_id or tweet_id so no one shard becomes a hotspot.

### Entity: `follows`
- `follower_id`
- `followee_id`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Needs efficient lookup both directions: 'who does X follow' (for fan-out on post) and 'who follows X' (also for fan-out on post), so this is typically indexed both ways or stored in two denormalized tables.

### Entity: `timeline_cache`
- `user_id (key)`
- `tweet_ids (an ordered list, the pre-computed feed)`
*Notes:* This is the pre-computed home timeline for regular users, built by fan-out-on-write. Celebrity tweets are deliberately excluded from this and merged in at read time instead.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read: the central trade-off of this whole system
Fan-out on write means: when a tweet is posted, immediately push it into the pre-computed timeline of every follower. Reads become trivial (just read your own pre-built list), but a single celebrity tweet triggers tens of millions of writes at once. Fan-out on read means: store nothing extra at write time, and when a user opens their timeline, pull recent tweets live from everyone they follow and merge them on the fly. Writes stay cheap regardless of follower count, but reads become expensive, since a user follows hundreds of people and each read has to fan out across all of them.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure fan-out on write: fast, cheap reads for everyone, but breaks catastrophically for celebrity accounts (50 million writes for one tweet)
- Pure fan-out on read: cheap, bounded writes always, but every single timeline read becomes an expensive scatter-gather across hundreds of followees, which doesn't scale for the far more frequent read path
- The real answer used in production systems: hybrid. Fan-out on write for accounts under some follower threshold (say 10,000), fan-out on read (merged live) for accounts above it. This bounds the worst-case write cost while keeping reads cheap for the vast majority of the traffic.

### How do you keep the pre-computed timeline from growing forever?
The timeline_cache for a user doesn't need to store their entire history, just enough recent tweet IDs to serve the first several pages (say, the most recent 800 tweet IDs). Older entries can be trimmed on write, and if a user scrolls back further than what's cached, that older portion falls back to a live, more expensive read, which is rare enough in practice to be acceptable.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Capping the cached timeline length keeps memory bounded per user regardless of how long the platform has existed
- Deep scroll-back becomes slower (falls back to live fan-out-on-read style merge), but this is a rare access pattern, most engagement happens on recent tweets

### How do you generate tweet IDs that are both unique and roughly sortable by time, without a central bottleneck?
A naive auto-increment ID needs a single source of truth, which becomes a write bottleneck at this scale. A Snowflake-style ID (timestamp bits + machine/shard ID bits + a per-machine sequence number, packed into a 64-bit integer) lets every app server generate globally unique, roughly time-sortable IDs independently, with no coordination needed between servers at all.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Snowflake-style IDs: no central bottleneck, IDs sort roughly by creation time (useful for pagination), but clock skew between machines can cause minor, generally harmless, ordering imperfections
- A centralized ID-generation service: perfectly ordered, but becomes exactly the kind of single bottleneck this design is trying to avoid at high write volume

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Celebrity accounts remain the sharpest edge case even with the hybrid fan-out approach; a threshold that's too low still causes large fan-out spikes, so the threshold itself may need to be dynamic based on real follower count and posting frequency.
- The follows table can grow to tens of billions of rows; it needs to be sharded (commonly by follower_id, since 'who do I follow' is the hotter read path during fan-out) and indexed for both directions of lookup.
- The timeline_cache, being read on nearly every app open, needs to live in a distributed in-memory store (like Redis Cluster) rather than a disk-backed database, and that store itself needs to be sharded by user_id to spread load.
- At extreme scale, even the fan-out service can fall behind during a viral moment; a message queue between 'tweet posted' and 'fan-out workers' absorbs bursts instead of dropping or blocking on them, letting fan-out catch up asynchronously rather than failing.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing pure fan-out-on-write without accounting for celebrity accounts, then discovering the design falls over on the very first example an interviewer brings up.
- ⚠️ Trying to make the timeline strictly, perfectly real-time and consistent, which is a far harder (and usually unnecessary) problem than the actual product needs.
- ⚠️ Using a simple auto-increment primary key for tweet IDs at this scale, creating a single write bottleneck that has nothing to do with the interesting parts of the problem.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that 'who does X follow' and 'who follows X' are both extremely hot queries in opposite directions, and only indexing one direction.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't strict real-time consistency matter much for a home timeline?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the product experience of seeing a new tweet 2-3 seconds after it was posted is indistinguishable from seeing it instantly to almost every user, but designing for strict real-time consistency across a distributed fan-out system at this scale would require expensive coordination that provides no meaningful user-facing benefit. This is a textbook case where relaxing a non-functional requirement unlocks a much cheaper, much more scalable design.

**Q: How would you decide the follower-count threshold for switching from fan-out-on-write to fan-out-on-read?**

> **Model Answer:** By estimating the cost of a fan-out write burst at a given follower count against your queue/worker throughput, and picking a threshold where even the largest expected accounts above it don't overwhelm the live-merge read path at typical read volume. In practice this is tuned empirically and can be made dynamic, e.g. based on a combination of follower count and how frequently that account posts.

# Design Instagram

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Instagram • Meta` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Twitter's hard part is fanning out a tiny piece of text; Instagram's hard part starts a full step earlier, at **upload**, where a single photo has to be transcoded into half a dozen derivative sizes before it can appear anywhere, and the feed itself splits into two genuinely different retrieval systems: a deterministic follow-graph **home feed** and a ranked, recommendation-driven **Explore feed** that has nothing to do with who you follow.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a simplified version of Instagram: users can upload photos, follow
other users, see a home feed of recent photos from people they follow, and
browse an Explore page of recommended photos from accounts they do not
follow. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Are we designing for photos only, or do we also need to support video?

# Design a News Feed System (Facebook-style)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Facebook / Meta` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The fan-out question a follow-graph feed already has to answer is secondary here; the real fight is where a personalized **ranking score** gets computed, at write time when it is cheap but cannot see the viewer or the ad inventory, or at read time when it is expensive but can score every candidate against the exact person looking and the exact ads available right now.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a news feed system like Facebook's: users have friends and follow
pages and groups, and the feed they see is not simple reverse-chronological
order, it is ranked, mixing organic content from friends, pages, and groups
with sponsored posts (ads), based on a relevance score computed for that
specific viewer. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is the feed pure reverse-chronological, or does it need to be ranked by relevance?
*Why it matters:* Chronological is the fan-out problem another case study already solves. Ranking adds an entirely separate scoring layer that has to run somewhere in the pipeline, and where it runs shapes the whole architecture.

#### Q: What signals does ranking use, and how fresh do they need to be? Likes and comments from minutes ago, or a model retrained daily?
*Why it matters:* If ranking needs signals from the last few minutes (a friend just commented on a post), the scoring step cannot be a stale, precomputed batch job, it has to touch something closer to real time.

#### Q: Do ads need to be mixed into the feed, and if so, do they need real-time auction logic (budget pacing, frequency capping) or can they be inserted at fixed positions?
*Why it matters:* Real-time ad auctions add a second ranking system that must be merged with organic ranking on the read path, which is a materially different and harder problem than simply reserving every fifth slot for an ad.

#### Q: How large is a typical candidate pool per feed request, meaning how many friends, pages, and groups does an average user follow?
*Why it matters:* If a user follows thousands of sources, scoring every single one of their recent posts with a heavy model on every feed load is computationally infeasible, which forces a multi-stage ranking funnel rather than a single scoring pass.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can post to their own timeline, visible to friends.
- A user can view a ranked home feed mixing posts from friends, followed pages, and joined groups.
- The feed must interleave sponsored posts (ads) among organic content according to some placement policy.
- User interactions (likes, comments, shares, hides) must feed back into future ranking as signals.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Feed generation must complete quickly, well under a second, even though ranking is far more computationally expensive than pure chronological ordering.**
- **Ranking must incorporate near-real-time signals, a friend's comment from a minute ago should be able to influence what is shown right now, not tomorrow.**
- **Ad insertion must respect frequency caps and budget pacing without adding unacceptable latency to the read path.**
- **Ranking must degrade gracefully under system overload, falling back to a cheaper scoring method rather than failing the feed request entirely.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 1 billion daily active users
- Each daily active user opens their feed roughly 8 times a day
- An average user's candidate pool (recent posts from friends, pages, and groups they follow) is about 1,500 unread items at any given feed load
- A full ML ranking pass costs meaningfully more compute per item than a lightweight heuristic pass

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Feed requests per day:** 1,000,000,000 * 8 = 8 billion feed loads/day ≈ 92,593 requests/sec average, well above that at peak hours
- **Naive full-ranking scoring load:** 8,000,000,000 * 1,500 candidates = 12 trillion candidate scoring operations/day if every candidate got the expensive model on every request, this is the number that makes single-stage ranking impossible
- **After a cheap first-pass filter (1,500 -> 300 candidates):** 8,000,000,000 * 300 = 2.4 trillion heavy-model scoring operations/day ≈ 27.8 million/sec average, still enormous, requiring a large dedicated ranking service fleet
- **After a final shortlist for the expensive pass (300 -> 50 for final precise scoring):** 8,000,000,000 * 50 = 400 billion final-stage scoring operations/day ≈ 4.6 million/sec average, the volume the most accurate (and most expensive) model actually needs to handle

*Capacity Takeaway:* Scoring every candidate with a full ranking model on every feed load is computationally impossible at **12 trillion operations/day**, so the single fact that drives this architecture is that ranking has to be a **funnel**, cheap candidate generation and light filtering first, progressively narrowing the pool, with the most expensive and most accurate scoring reserved for only the last few hundred candidates.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A write path looks similar to a follow-graph feed: a post is created, and a
fan-out step pushes it into a bounded candidate_pool for each interested
user (friends, page followers, group members), the same mechanism used for
chronological feeds, just feeding a candidate pool rather than the final
feed. A read path is where this system diverges: a feed request pulls that
user's candidate pool (on the order of a thousand items), a lightweight
first-pass ranker cheaply scores and narrows it to a few hundred, a heavier
ranking model scores that shortlist using richer features (affinity,
recency, content type, predicted engagement), and in parallel an ad-serving
service returns eligible ads for that user respecting budget and frequency
caps. A final merge step interleaves ranked organic posts and ads according
to placement policy before the feed is returned.

    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Parallel ad auction (budget pacing, frequency caps)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Merge organic and ads (final ordered feed returned)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Where the ranking score gets computed

#### Ranking funnel: candidates narrowed per stage

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts

| `POST` | `/api/posts` | Creates a new post from the authenticated user, visible to friends, followers of their page, or group members depending on context. |

| `GET` | `/api/feed/refresh` | Returns newly available top-of-feed items since the last fetch, without disrupting the user's current scroll position. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `posts`
- `post_id (unique, time-sortable)`
- `author_id, source_type (friend, page, group)`
- `text/media references`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* The source of truth for content, independent of ranking, sharded by author_id or post_id.

### Entity: `edges_and_affinity`
- `user_id`
- `source_id (friend, page, or group)`
- `affinity_score (how often this user engages with this source, decayed over time)`
*Notes:* A per-user, per-source relationship strength score, one of the core ranking features, updated incrementally as interactions happen rather than recomputed from scratch.

### Entity: `candidate_pool`
- `user_id (key)`
- `candidate_post_ids (recent unseen posts from followed sources)`
*Notes:* A precomputed, bounded pool per user, built similarly to a fan-out-on-write timeline, that acts as the input to the ranking funnel rather than the final feed itself.

### Entity: `ad_campaigns`
- `campaign_id`
- `targeting_criteria`
- `budget_remaining, frequency_cap`
- `bid_value`
*Notes:* Managed and queried by a separate ad-serving system that runs its own ranking/auction and is merged with organic ranking results at read time.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Where does the ranking score actually get computed: write time or read time?
Write-time (precomputed) ranking would mean scoring a post for every potential viewer as soon as it is created and storing a per-viewer ordered feed, similar to a fan-out-on-write timeline cache. Read-time ranking means storing only a candidate pool at write time, and computing the actual relevance score fresh, for the specific viewer, at the moment they request their feed.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Pure write-time scoring: reads become nearly free, just fetch a pre-ordered list, but a score computed once at write time cannot react to the viewer's identity, cannot incorporate ad auction results happening right now, and goes stale the moment new engagement signals arrive on that post
- Pure read-time scoring: always fresh and fully personalized to the exact viewer and the current ad inventory, but scoring a viewer's entire candidate pool live, for every single feed load, is the 12-trillion-operations-a-day problem from the capacity estimate
- The real answer used in production: a hybrid funnel. Candidate generation (which content exists that this user might care about) happens near write time and is cheap to maintain incrementally, like a timeline cache; the actual relevance scoring happens at read time, but only against that already-narrowed candidate pool, so read-time cost is bounded to hundreds of candidates, not the full firehose of everything followed sources have posted

### Why can't a single ranking model score every candidate on every request?
A highly accurate ranking model (deep learning based, using dozens of features per candidate) is expensive to run per item. Running it against a full candidate pool of roughly 1,500 items per feed load, across 8 billion feed loads a day, is not computationally feasible at any reasonable cost. The solution used at this scale is a multi-stage funnel: a very cheap heuristic or lightweight model narrows 1,500 candidates down to a few hundred, then a mid-cost model narrows further, and only the final, small shortlist gets the most expensive and most accurate model.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Single-stage full-model ranking on every candidate: theoretically the most accurate ranking possible, but computationally impossible at this scale, this is not a real option in production
- A multi-stage funnel (cheap filter, then mid-cost model, then expensive final ranker on a small shortlist): each stage trades a small amount of ranking accuracy (a genuinely relevant post might get filtered out early by a cheap heuristic) for a large reduction in compute, and the funnel shape is tuned so the final expensive stage only ever sees a shortlist small enough to score within the request's latency budget
- The risk of a funnel is a good candidate getting incorrectly dropped at an early cheap stage and never reaching the accurate final ranker; this is mitigated by making the early stages deliberately conservative (over-include rather than under-include) since compute is cheaper than losing a genuinely relevant post

### How do organic content and ads get merged into a single feed?
Organic ranking and ad ranking are computed by separate systems with different objectives: organic ranking optimizes for predicted engagement/relevance to the viewer, ad ranking optimizes for a combination of bid value, predicted engagement, and budget pacing for the advertiser. Both need to be reconciled into one ordered feed the user actually scrolls through.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Fixed-position insertion (an ad every N organic posts, computed after ranking each independently): simple to reason about and easy to guarantee frequency caps, but does not adapt ad placement based on how strong or weak the surrounding organic content's relevance is
- Score-based blended merge (ads and organic posts scored on comparable normalized scales and merged by score, subject to frequency-cap and pacing constraints): can place a highly relevant ad above weaker organic content, closer to a genuinely unified ranking, but requires normalizing two very differently computed scores onto the same scale, which is a real modeling challenge, not just an engineering one
- In practice this merge step runs as its own service, called in parallel with organic ranking so it does not add serial latency, then blends the two ranked lists just before the feed response is assembled, keeping ad-serving logic decoupled from organic ranking logic

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The ranking service fleet is the single largest compute cost in this system by far, given trillions of scoring operations a day even after funnel narrowing; it needs to scale horizontally and independently of the app servers that just orchestrate the request.
- A feature store (holding affinity scores, recency signals, engagement counts) needs to serve very low-latency reads during ranking, since ranking hundreds of candidates per request means hundreds of feature lookups per request, this typically needs its own in-memory or specialized low-latency store, not the primary database.
- Candidate generation, though cheaper than ranking, still needs to stay fresh as new posts arrive continuously; a lagging candidate pool means genuinely new content simply never gets a chance to be ranked.
- Ad auction and organic ranking calls run in parallel, but the read path's total latency is bounded by whichever is slower, so both need aggressive timeout and fallback behavior (serve organic-only, or a cached feed) rather than blocking the whole request on a slow ranking or ad call.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming a ranked feed is just a chronological feed with a sort function applied at the end, missing that the actual scoring step (with real features and a real model) is the majority of the system's cost.
- ⚠️ ==Proposing to score every candidate with the most accurate model on every single request== without doing the arithmetic on how many scoring operations that implies at real scale.
- ⚠️ Treating ad insertion as an afterthought (just reserve a slot every few posts) when the system explicitly requires respecting **budget pacing** and **frequency caps**, which needs its own service and a real merge step.
- ⚠️ ==Precomputing a single ranked feed at write time== as if it were a Twitter-style timeline cache, forgetting that relevance ranking is inherently viewer-specific and needs to react to signals newer than the post itself.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't the home feed just be precomputed once per post the way a chronological timeline cache is?**

> **Model Answer:** Because relevance ranking depends on the viewer, not just the poster: the same post should rank differently for two different friends based on their individual affinity scores, recent engagement patterns, and even what ads are competing for that viewer's attention right now. A single precomputed score per post cannot capture any of that, so the actual scoring step has to happen per viewer, at read time, against a candidate pool that was cheaply prepared in advance.

**Q: How would you handle a ranking service outage without taking down the entire feed?**

> **Model Answer:** Define a fallback ranking mode, for example a much cheaper heuristic (recency plus a static affinity score) that can run even if the full ranking model service is unavailable or overloaded, and have the app server time out and fall back to it rather than blocking the request indefinitely. A slightly worse-ranked feed is a far better outcome than a failed feed request, since the product's core promise is showing something relevant quickly, not showing the theoretically optimal ranking every time.

- The risk of a funnel is a good candidate getting incorrectly dropped at an early cheap stage and never reaching the accurate final ranker; this is mitigated by making the early stages deliberately conservative (over-include rather than under-include) since compute is cheaper than losing a genuinely relevant post

### How do organic content and ads get merged into a single feed?
Organic ranking and ad ranking are computed by separate systems with different objectives: organic ranking optimizes for predicted engagement/relevance to the viewer, ad ranking optimizes for a combination of bid value, predicted engagement, and budget pacing for the advertiser. Both need to be reconciled into one ordered feed the user actually scrolls through.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Fixed-position insertion (an ad every N organic posts, computed after ranking each independently): simple to reason about and easy to guarantee frequency caps, but does not adapt ad placement based on how strong or weak the surrounding organic content's relevance is
- Score-based blended merge (ads and organic posts scored on comparable normalized scales and merged by score, subject to frequency-cap and pacing constraints): can place a highly relevant ad above weaker organic content, closer to a genuinely unified ranking, but requires normalizing two very differently computed scores onto the same scale, which is a real modeling challenge, not just an engineering one
- In practice this merge step runs as its own service, called in parallel with organic ranking so it does not add serial latency, then blends the two ranked lists just before the feed response is assembled, keeping ad-serving logic decoupled from organic ranking logic

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The ranking service fleet is the single largest compute cost in this system by far, given trillions of scoring operations a day even after funnel narrowing; it needs to scale horizontally and independently of the app servers that just orchestrate the request.
- A feature store (holding affinity scores, recency signals, engagement counts) needs to serve very low-latency reads during ranking, since ranking hundreds of candidates per request means hundreds of feature lookups per request, this typically needs its own in-memory or specialized low-latency store, not the primary database.
- Candidate generation, though cheaper than ranking, still needs to stay fresh as new posts arrive continuously; a lagging candidate pool means genuinely new content simply never gets a chance to be ranked.
- Ad auction and organic ranking calls run in parallel, but the read path's total latency is bounded by whichever is slower, so both need aggressive timeout and fallback behavior (serve organic-only, or a cached feed) rather than blocking the whole request on a slow ranking or ad call.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Assuming a ranked feed is just a chronological feed with a sort function applied at the end, missing that the actual scoring step (with real features and a real model) is the majority of the system's cost.
- ⚠️ ==Proposing to score every candidate with the most accurate model on every single request== without doing the arithmetic on how many scoring operations that implies at real scale.
- ⚠️ Treating ad insertion as an afterthought (just reserve a slot every few posts) when the system explicitly requires respecting **budget pacing** and **frequency caps**, which needs its own service and a real merge step.
- ⚠️ ==Precomputing a single ranked feed at write time== as if it were a Twitter-style timeline cache, forgetting that relevance ranking is inherently viewer-specific and needs to react to signals newer than the post itself.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't the home feed just be precomputed once per post the way a chronological timeline cache is?**

> **Model Answer:** Because relevance ranking depends on the viewer, not just the poster: the same post should rank differently for two different friends based on their individual affinity scores, recent engagement patterns, and even what ads are competing for that viewer's attention right now. A single precomputed score per post cannot capture any of that, so the actual scoring step has to happen per viewer, at read time, against a candidate pool that was cheaply prepared in advance.

**Q: How would you handle a ranking service outage without taking down the entire feed?**

> **Model Answer:** Define a fallback ranking mode, for example a much cheaper heuristic (recency plus a static affinity score) that can run even if the full ranking model service is unavailable or overloaded, and have the app server time out and fall back to it rather than blocking the request indefinitely. A slightly worse-ranked feed is a far better outcome than a failed feed request, since the product's core promise is showing something relevant quickly, not showing the theoretically optimal ranking every time.

# Design Reddit

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Reddit` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> There is no single global timeline to fan out here at all: every feed is **scoped to a subreddit**, so the hard problem shifts from 'who do I push this to' toward 'how do millions of concurrent vote taps update a ranking score without a hot post's row becoming a ==write bottleneck==.'

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a simplified version of Reddit: users can create communities
(subreddits), post text/link/image posts into a specific subreddit, upvote
or downvote posts and comments, and browse a subreddit's posts sorted by
hot, top, or new. Posts also have nested, threaded comments. Design the
system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is a user's home page an aggregation across all subreddits they've joined, or is browsing always done one subreddit at a time?
*Why it matters:* A per-subreddit feed is a bounded, indexable query. An aggregated home feed across an arbitrary set of joined subreddits is closer to a **fan-in merge problem**, and changes whether we can get away with simple per-subreddit sorted indexes or need a separate aggregation layer.

#### Q: How is a 'hot' ranking computed, does it need to match Reddit's actual time-decay formula, or can we define our own scoring function?
*Why it matters:* The **scoring formula** decides whether ranking can be computed once and cached (a formula that only depends on vote count and post age) or needs continuous recomputation. It also determines whether we can maintain a sorted structure incrementally or must re-sort on every read.

#### Q: How deep can comment threads nest, and roughly how large can a single post's comment tree get?
*Why it matters:* A shallow, ==capped nesting depth== lets us store a parent pointer and paginate reasonably. A post with hundreds of thousands of comments in a deep tree (a common occurrence on large subreddits) needs a storage and pagination strategy that doesn't require loading the whole tree to render any part of it.

#### Q: Do votes need to be exact and immediately reflected, or is a brief lag on the displayed count acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Exact, immediate vote counts on a viral post require every single vote to hit a strongly consistent counter, which becomes a ==serialization point== under a flood of taps. Accepting a few seconds of lag opens the door to **batched, asynchronous counter updates** that scale far better.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a subreddit and post text, link, or image posts into it.
- A user can upvote or downvote a post or a comment, and change or remove their vote.
- A user can view a subreddit's posts sorted by **hot, top, or new**.
- A user can post a comment on a post, or reply to another comment, forming a nested thread.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Reading a subreddit's front page must be fast, well under a second, even for subreddits with tens of millions of subscribers.**
- **Vote counts must stay accurate under extremely high concurrent write volume on a single popular post, without the vote-counting mechanism becoming a ==bottleneck==.**
- **The system must prevent a single user's account (or a coordinated group of accounts) from trivially inflating vote counts, i.e. some abuse resistance is expected, even if full detection is out of scope.**
- **High availability for reads: a subreddit page should always render, even if the hot ranking is a few seconds stale, rather than error out.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50 million daily active users
- 2 million posts created per day across all subreddits; each daily active user casts an average of 20 votes a day
- The top 1% of posts (by subreddit size and timing) receive 90% of total vote volume, i.e. votes are heavily concentrated on a small number of hot posts
- Each daily active user views 10 subreddit or post pages a day

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Posts created per day:** 2,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 23 writes/sec average, trivially low
- **Votes cast per day:** 50,000,000 * 20 = 1 billion votes/day ≈ 11,570 votes/sec average
- **Peak vote rate on a single viral post:** If 90% of 1 billion votes land on the top 1% of 2,000,000 posts (20,000 posts), that's 900,000,000 / 20,000 ≈ 45,000 votes per hot post per day, and a genuinely viral post can see thousands of votes in a single minute, i.e. tens of votes per second hitting one row
- **Page reads per day:** 50,000,000 * 10 = 500 million reads/day ≈ 5,787 reads/sec average, roughly 50:1 reads to writes overall

*Capacity Takeaway:* Total vote volume looks modest on average, around 11,500 votes a second platform-wide, but the real constraint is **concentration**: a single viral post can absorb tens of votes per second on one row, which is why counting votes has to be ==decoupled== from incrementing a single database row synchronously.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A write path for votes: a client casts a vote, the app server **upserts a row**
in the votes table (unique per user per target, so it's idempotent and
reversible), and asynchronously publishes a vote-delta event onto a queue
rather than incrementing the post's counter synchronously. A pool of
**counting workers** consumes that queue, batches deltas per post over a short
window (a second or two), and applies them as a single aggregated update to
the post's upvotes/downvotes and hot_score. A read path for a subreddit
feed: the app server queries a sorted index on (subreddit_id, hot_score) or
(subreddit_id, created_at) depending on the requested sort, which never
requires scanning or re-ranking at read time. A read path for comments:
fetch top-level comments for a post ordered by the requested sort, then
lazily fetch child replies per thread as the user expands them, rather than
loading the entire tree in one response.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Vote counting pipeline and subreddit feed reads

flowchart LR

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    votesdb[("Votes Store")]:::db
    queue>"Vote Delta Queue"]:::queue
    worker["Counting Workers"]:::server
    postsdb[("Posts Store (hot_score)")]:::db
    cache["Subreddit Feed Cache"]:::cache
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"upsert vote"| votesdb
    app -.->|"publish vote delta"| queue
    queue -.-> worker
    worker -.->|"batched counter + hot_score update"| postsdb
    postsdb -.->|"refresh sorted index"| cache
    app -->|"read subreddit feed"| cache
```

#### Upserting a vote

  a["Vote request arrives"] --> b{"Existing vote row?"}
  b -->|"no"| c["Insert vote row"]
  b -->|"yes, same direction"| d["Remove vote (toggle off)"]
  b -->|"yes, opposite direction"| e["Update vote row"]
  c --> f["Publish delta to queue"]
  d --> f
  e --> f
```

#### Hot score decays linearly with post age

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/subreddits/{name}/posts` | Body: { type, title, body_or_url }. Creates a new post in the named subreddit. |
| `POST` | `/api/posts/{postId}/vote` | Body: { direction: up | down | none }. Casts, changes, or removes the authenticated user's vote on a post. |
| `GET` | `/api/subreddits/{name}?sort=hot|top|new` | Returns a paginated, sorted list of posts for the subreddit. |
| `GET` | `/api/posts/{postId}/comments` | Returns the nested comment tree for a post, paginated by top-level thread. |
| `POST` | `/api/comments/{commentId}/reply` | Body: { text }. Creates a reply nested under the given comment. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `subreddits`
- `subreddit_id`
- `name (unique, indexed)`
- `subscriber_count`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The scoping unit for every feed query; almost every read in this system starts with a subreddit_id filter.

### Entity: `posts`
- `post_id (time-sortable)`
- `subreddit_id (indexed)`
- `author_id`
- `title, body_or_url`
- `upvotes, downvotes (approximate counters)`
- `hot_score (precomputed, periodically refreshed)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* ==hot_score== is not recomputed on every read; it's recalculated on a schedule (or on a large enough vote delta) from vote count and post age, and a sorted index on (subreddit_id, hot_score) serves the hot feed directly.

### Entity: `votes`
- `user_id`
- `target_id (post or comment)`
- `target_type (post, comment)`
- `direction (up, down)`
*Notes:* One row per user per target, **unique on (user_id, target_id)**, so a repeated vote updates rather than duplicates, this is what makes vote changes and removals possible and prevents trivial double-voting from the same account.

### Entity: `comments`
- `comment_id (time-sortable)`
- `post_id (indexed)`
- `parent_comment_id (nullable, for top-level comments)`
- `author_id, text`
- `upvotes, downvotes`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* parent_comment_id forms the **thread tree**; depth is capped at the application layer (say 10 levels) to keep rendering and pagination bounded.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you count votes on a viral post without a single row becoming a write bottleneck?
The naive approach is `UPDATE posts SET upvotes = upvotes + 1 WHERE post_id = X` on every vote, which serializes every vote on that post through a single row lock. Under a burst of tens of votes per second on one row, that ==lock contention== becomes the bottleneck, not the total system throughput.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous per-vote row update: counts are always exactly correct and instantly visible, but a single hot post directly bottlenecks on **database row-lock contention** under load
- Asynchronous batched counting via a queue and periodic aggregation: absorbs bursts smoothly and scales independently of any single post's popularity, but the displayed count lags real votes by up to the batching window (a second or two), which is an acceptable trade for a vote counter
- A middle ground: an in-memory counter (e.g. a Redis atomic increment) per post that's cheap to increment at high frequency, periodically flushed to the durable posts table, giving near-real-time counts without hammering the primary database directly

### How do you compute and serve the hot ranking without re-sorting every post on every read?
A 'hot' score that blends **vote count and post age** (so a post with fewer votes but posted five minutes ago can outrank an older post with more votes) changes continuously just from the passage of time, not just from new votes, which means a naive design might try to recompute it live on every feed read.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Recompute hot_score live at read time for every post in the result set: always perfectly fresh, but multiplies read cost by however many posts are being ranked, and that cost is paid on every single feed load
- Precompute hot_score periodically (e.g. every few minutes, or triggered by a large vote delta) and maintain a sorted index on it: reads become a cheap indexed range scan, at the cost of the ranking being briefly stale between recomputations
- In practice, precomputed and periodically refreshed wins for any subreddit above trivial size, since the staleness window is invisible to users scrolling a feed, but the read cost savings are not

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A small number of extremely large subreddits (the equivalent of celebrity accounts here) generate ==disproportionate== read and vote traffic; their post indexes and hot-score computation may need dedicated capacity separate from the long tail of small subreddits.
- The votes table grows to tens of billions of rows and is queried both by target_id (to get a post's counts) and by user_id (to know how the current user already voted, for UI state); it needs indexes supporting both access patterns, and likely **sharding by target_id** since that's the hotter path.
- Deep comment threads on a massively popular post can reach hundreds of thousands of nodes; lazy, paginated loading per branch (rather than ever materializing the full tree) is required, and a capped nesting depth keeps both storage and rendering bounded.
- The counting-worker queue itself can fall behind during a coordinated brigading event or a genuinely massive viral spike; it needs to scale horizontally and should degrade to showing a slightly staler count rather than backing up indefinitely.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Updating a post's vote counter synchronously on every single vote==, which creates exactly the kind of row-lock bottleneck that breaks down first on the platform's most popular posts.
- ⚠️ ==Treating a user's vote as a simple insert rather than an upsert==, which allows the same user to vote multiple times or makes changing a vote impossible to represent cleanly.
- ⚠️ Recomputing the hot ranking for an entire subreddit on every single feed read instead of precomputing and periodically refreshing it.
- ⚠️ Loading an entire comment tree in one response for a heavily discussed post, instead of paginating and lazily expanding branches.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is batching vote updates through a queue better than incrementing a counter directly, given that it makes counts briefly stale?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the bottleneck under load isn't total vote volume, it's **contention on a single row** for a single popular post. A queue with batched aggregation lets many votes on the same post be absorbed and merged into one write, decoupling vote-arrival rate from write rate on that row. A few seconds of staleness on a vote count is invisible to users, while row-lock contention directly causes visible latency or failed votes.

**Q: How would you support a user changing their vote from up to down, and why does the votes table need a unique constraint per user per target?**

> **Model Answer:** The vote endpoint **upserts on (user_id, target_id)**: if a row already exists, it's updated in place rather than inserted again, and the delta published downstream reflects the net change (e.g. -1 for the removed upvote and -1 for the new downvote, a swing of 2). Without that unique constraint, a user could accumulate multiple vote rows for the same target, making counts wrong and vote removal ambiguous.

- `parent_comment_id (nullable, for top-level comments)`
- `author_id, text`
- `upvotes, downvotes`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* parent_comment_id forms the **thread tree**; depth is capped at the application layer (say 10 levels) to keep rendering and pagination bounded.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you count votes on a viral post without a single row becoming a write bottleneck?
The naive approach is `UPDATE posts SET upvotes = upvotes + 1 WHERE post_id = X` on every vote, which serializes every vote on that post through a single row lock. Under a burst of tens of votes per second on one row, that ==lock contention== becomes the bottleneck, not the total system throughput.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous per-vote row update: counts are always exactly correct and instantly visible, but a single hot post directly bottlenecks on **database row-lock contention** under load
- Asynchronous batched counting via a queue and periodic aggregation: absorbs bursts smoothly and scales independently of any single post's popularity, but the displayed count lags real votes by up to the batching window (a second or two), which is an acceptable trade for a vote counter
- A middle ground: an in-memory counter (e.g. a Redis atomic increment) per post that's cheap to increment at high frequency, periodically flushed to the durable posts table, giving near-real-time counts without hammering the primary database directly

### How do you compute and serve the hot ranking without re-sorting every post on every read?
A 'hot' score that blends **vote count and post age** (so a post with fewer votes but posted five minutes ago can outrank an older post with more votes) changes continuously just from the passage of time, not just from new votes, which means a naive design might try to recompute it live on every feed read.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Recompute hot_score live at read time for every post in the result set: always perfectly fresh, but multiplies read cost by however many posts are being ranked, and that cost is paid on every single feed load
- Precompute hot_score periodically (e.g. every few minutes, or triggered by a large vote delta) and maintain a sorted index on it: reads become a cheap indexed range scan, at the cost of the ranking being briefly stale between recomputations
- In practice, precomputed and periodically refreshed wins for any subreddit above trivial size, since the staleness window is invisible to users scrolling a feed, but the read cost savings are not

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A small number of extremely large subreddits (the equivalent of celebrity accounts here) generate ==disproportionate== read and vote traffic; their post indexes and hot-score computation may need dedicated capacity separate from the long tail of small subreddits.
- The votes table grows to tens of billions of rows and is queried both by target_id (to get a post's counts) and by user_id (to know how the current user already voted, for UI state); it needs indexes supporting both access patterns, and likely **sharding by target_id** since that's the hotter path.
- Deep comment threads on a massively popular post can reach hundreds of thousands of nodes; lazy, paginated loading per branch (rather than ever materializing the full tree) is required, and a capped nesting depth keeps both storage and rendering bounded.
- The counting-worker queue itself can fall behind during a coordinated brigading event or a genuinely massive viral spike; it needs to scale horizontally and should degrade to showing a slightly staler count rather than backing up indefinitely.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Updating a post's vote counter synchronously on every single vote==, which creates exactly the kind of row-lock bottleneck that breaks down first on the platform's most popular posts.
- ⚠️ ==Treating a user's vote as a simple insert rather than an upsert==, which allows the same user to vote multiple times or makes changing a vote impossible to represent cleanly.
- ⚠️ Recomputing the hot ranking for an entire subreddit on every single feed read instead of precomputing and periodically refreshing it.
- ⚠️ Loading an entire comment tree in one response for a heavily discussed post, instead of paginating and lazily expanding branches.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is batching vote updates through a queue better than incrementing a counter directly, given that it makes counts briefly stale?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the bottleneck under load isn't total vote volume, it's **contention on a single row** for a single popular post. A queue with batched aggregation lets many votes on the same post be absorbed and merged into one write, decoupling vote-arrival rate from write rate on that row. A few seconds of staleness on a vote count is invisible to users, while row-lock contention directly causes visible latency or failed votes.

**Q: How would you support a user changing their vote from up to down, and why does the votes table need a unique constraint per user per target?**

> **Model Answer:** The vote endpoint **upserts on (user_id, target_id)**: if a row already exists, it's updated in place rather than inserted again, and the delta published downstream reflects the net change (e.g. -1 for the removed upvote and -1 for the new downvote, a swing of 2). Without that unique constraint, a user could accumulate multiple vote rows for the same target, making counts wrong and vote removal ambiguous.

# Design a Trending Topics / Hashtag System

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Twitter/X Trends • Google Trends` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This is not a database query problem at all, it's a **streaming problem**: with millions of distinct hashtags and a firehose of events, you can neither store an exact count for every possible term nor scan history on every request, so the entire design is about ==approximate, memory-bounded counting== over a moving time window rather than exact bookkeeping.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a system that shows what's trending right now: the top N hashtags
or topics by mention frequency over a recent sliding time window (for
example, the last hour), continuously updated as new posts stream in
across an enormous, high-volume event stream. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Does 'trending' mean the raw count of mentions, or a spike relative to a topic's normal baseline (so a topic that quadruples suddenly ranks above one that's merely popular every day)?
*Why it matters:* Raw frequency ranks the same handful of always-popular terms every day and rarely surfaces genuine news events. A **spike/velocity-based** definition requires tracking a baseline per topic over a longer window, which is a materially different and heavier computation than a simple top-N count.

#### Q: How large is the sliding window, and does it need to slide continuously (any arbitrary 'last hour' at any second) or can it be a series of fixed, discrete buckets (e.g. non-overlapping 1-minute buckets)?
*Why it matters:* A continuously sliding exact window requires expiring individual events at the second they age out, which is ==expensive at this volume==. **Fixed discrete buckets** that get summed and the oldest one dropped is far cheaper and is what real systems approximate a sliding window with.

#### Q: Is a small amount of counting error acceptable, or must every count be exact?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether an approximate structure like a **Count-Min Sketch** is even on the table. Exact counting of every distinct hashtag over a rolling window at this event volume requires storage and computation that doesn't fit in memory; a small, bounded overcount error is what makes the problem tractable.

#### Q: Roughly what's the event volume, and how skewed is the hashtag distribution (a handful of extremely hot topics versus a long tail of rare ones)?
*Why it matters:* Extreme skew (a **Zipfian distribution**, which is realistic for hashtags) is exactly the case an approximate counting structure like Count-Min Sketch is built for: it trades a little accuracy on rare items for huge memory savings, which only matters if the tail is genuinely long.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- The system ingests a high-volume stream of posts, each of which may contain zero or more hashtags/topics.
- The system maintains an **approximate count** of mentions per hashtag over a recent sliding time window (e.g. the last hour).
- The system serves a 'top N trending' list, continuously updated, ranked by count (or by spike/velocity if that's in scope).
- Old mentions age out of the window automatically; a hashtag that stops being mentioned eventually falls out of the trending list.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **The system must handle an extremely high and bursty event rate (tens to hundreds of thousands of mentions per second during major live events) without falling behind.**
- **Memory usage must stay **bounded** regardless of how many distinct hashtags ever appear, since exact per-hashtag storage over all history is infeasible.**
- **Reading the current trending list must be fast, well under a second, since it's polled or displayed extremely frequently.**
- **A small, bounded approximation error in counts is acceptable in exchange for constant, predictable memory usage.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 million posts per day platform-wide, average
- During a major live event (e.g. a big sports final), peak ingest is 20 times the daily average rate for a short burst
- Roughly 15% of posts contain at least one hashtag, averaging 1.3 hashtags per tagged post
- Millions of distinct hashtags exist across all history, but only tens of thousands are active in any given hour

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Average mention ingest rate:** 500,000,000 posts/day / 86,400 ≈ 5,787 posts/sec; 5,787 * 0.15 * 1.3 ≈ 1,128 hashtag mentions/sec average
- **Peak mention ingest rate during a live event:** 1,128 * 20 ≈ 22,560 hashtag mentions/sec at peak, which is the number the ingest pipeline must sustain, not the average
- **Exact counting memory cost (why it doesn't work):** If 2 million distinct hashtags are ever seen, storing exact counts (hashtag string + counter) even at ~40 bytes each is 2,000,000 * 40 ≈ 80 MB, which sounds fine until you need one such structure per time bucket per window, and the real number of distinct strings ever seen (including misspellings, unicode variants, spam) is far higher and unbounded over time
- **Count-Min Sketch memory cost (why it works):** A CMS with width 2000 and depth 5 (5 independent hash functions) uses 2000 * 5 = 10,000 counters, at 4 bytes each ≈ 40 KB per bucket, a fixed cost regardless of how many distinct hashtags exist, several orders of magnitude smaller than exact storage at this cardinality

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving fact is **cardinality, not raw event volume**: with potentially unbounded distinct hashtag strings over time, exact per-item counting doesn't fit in memory in any bounded way, which is why this is fundamentally a Count-Min Sketch (or similar probabilistic structure) problem, one fixed-size sketch per time bucket, rather than a counting-table problem.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
An ingest path: post-processing workers extract hashtags from each new
post and publish a lightweight mention event onto a stream (e.g. Kafka),
partitioned so ordering per hashtag isn't required, since counting is
**commutative**. A counting path: stream-processing workers consume mention
events in small time-aligned buckets (e.g. every 1 minute), updating that
bucket's **Count-Min Sketch** and, alongside it, a bounded top-K heap of
candidate heavy hitters for that bucket, so the system tracks "who might be
trending" without ever enumerating the full hashtag space. A window
computation path: to answer "what's trending in the last hour," the
counting service sums estimated counts for each heavy-hitter candidate
across the last N buckets that make up the window, drops buckets that have
aged out, and re-ranks. A read path: the current top-N list is cached and
served directly, refreshed every time a new bucket completes, so read
traffic never touches the sketches directly.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Streaming ingest, bucketed sketches, and cached trending reads

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["Post Ingest Servers"]:::server
    stream>"Mention Event Stream"]:::queue
    counter["Sketch Counting Workers"]:::server
    sketchdb["Bucket Sketch Store"]:::cache
    heavyhitters["Top-K Candidate Store"]:::cache
    trending["Trending List Cache"]:::cache
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -.->|"publish mention event"| stream
    stream -.-> counter
    counter -.->|"update bucket sketch"| sketchdb
    counter -.->|"update top-K candidates"| heavyhitters
    heavyhitters -.->|"recompute window ranking"| trending
    app -->|"read top-N trending"| trending
```

#### The bucket lifecycle behind a sliding window

#### Memory: exact counting vs Count-Min Sketch

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/trending?window=1h&limit=10` | Returns the current top-N trending hashtags for the given sliding window, most recent count estimate first. |
| `POST` | `/internal/events/mentions` | Internal ingest endpoint (or stream topic) that publishes a **{ hashtag, post_id, timestamp }** event for every hashtag extracted from a new post. |
| `GET` | `/api/topics/{hashtag}/history` | Returns a coarse-grained historical mention volume for a specific hashtag over recent buckets, for a topic detail view. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `bucket_sketches`
- `bucket_id (e.g. minute-aligned timestamp)`
- `sketch (a fixed-size Count-Min Sketch: an array of counter rows, one per hash function)`
*Notes:* One compact sketch per fixed time bucket (e.g. 1-minute buckets). The sliding window's count for a hashtag is the **sum of its estimated count** across all buckets currently inside the window; the oldest bucket is dropped as a new one is added, approximating a continuously sliding window with discrete steps.

### Entity: `heavy_hitters`
- `hashtag (indexed)`
- `window_id`
- `estimated_count`
*Notes:* A small, explicitly tracked candidate set (a **heap or top-K structure**) of hashtags likely to be trending, maintained alongside the sketch so the system doesn't need to enumerate every distinct hashtag ever seen to answer 'what's in the top 10 right now.'

### Entity: `topic_metadata`
- `hashtag (unique)`
- `first_seen_at`
- `category (nullable, e.g. sports, politics, entertainment)`
*Notes:* Lightweight metadata for display purposes only, not part of the counting hot path.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why use a Count-Min Sketch instead of an exact hash map of hashtag to count?
A Count-Min Sketch is a fixed-size 2D array of counters plus several independent hash functions. To increment a hashtag's count, it's hashed by each function and the corresponding counter in each row is incremented. To estimate a count, the same hashes are looked up and the **minimum across rows** is returned (minimum, because hash collisions can only inflate a counter, never deflate it, so the smallest observed value is the closest to truth).

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Exact hash map: perfectly accurate counts, but memory ==grows linearly== with the number of distinct hashtags ever seen, which is unbounded and, at real scale, includes huge amounts of spam and one-off noise
- Count-Min Sketch: fixed memory regardless of cardinality, and counts are guaranteed to only ever overestimate, never underestimate, but rare hashtags can occasionally get inflated counts from collisions, and there is no way to enumerate 'all hashtags' from the sketch alone, only to query counts for a known hashtag
- The practical answer, used here, combines both: the sketch handles counting at fixed memory cost, while a separate small top-K heavy-hitters structure (updated alongside it) tracks the candidate set of likely-trending hashtags explicitly, since the sketch alone can't produce a top-N list, only answer 'how many for this specific hashtag'

### How do you approximate a continuously sliding time window using discrete buckets, and what error does that introduce?
A perfectly exact 'last 60 minutes, updated every second' window would require ==expiring individual mention events== the instant they age past exactly 60 minutes ago, which means tracking and later removing every individual event, defeating the whole point of using a compact sketch. Instead, time is divided into fixed buckets (e.g. 1-minute buckets), each with its own sketch, and the window's count is the sum across the last 60 buckets, with the oldest bucket dropped and a new one added every minute.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Continuously exact sliding window: no staleness at the boundary, but requires per-event expiration bookkeeping that is exactly the unbounded-memory problem this design is trying to avoid
- Fixed discrete buckets (e.g. 1-minute granularity): the window updates in visible steps rather than continuously, so a mention that just aged out of the oldest bucket disappears all at once rather than gradually, but this granularity is invisible to users looking at a trending list and makes the whole computation a cheap sum over a fixed number of small sketches
- Smaller buckets (e.g. 10 seconds) reduce the step-change granularity at the cost of more sketches to sum per query; the bucket size is a tunable trade-off between smoothness and per-query computation cost

### Raw mention count versus spike/velocity ranking: what actually counts as 'trending'?
Ranking purely by mention count in the window means the same perpetually popular topics (a huge fanbase's daily hashtag, for instance) dominate the trending list every single day, which isn't what users mean by 'trending', they mean **something unusual happening right now**.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Raw count ranking: simple, cheap, directly derived from the sketch sum, but surfaces the same evergreen topics repeatedly and rarely reflects breaking news
- Spike/velocity ranking (current window count versus a rolling baseline average for that same hashtag): surfaces genuine anomalies and breaking events, which is what users actually expect from a 'trending' feature, but requires maintaining a longer-running baseline per candidate hashtag, which is more storage and computation on top of the sketch
- A practical middle ground: use raw sketch counts to cheaply narrow down to a top-K candidate set per bucket, then only compute the more expensive baseline/velocity comparison for that small candidate set, not for every hashtag ever seen

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The mention ingest stream is the ==first pressure point== during a live event; it needs to be partitioned (e.g. by hashtag hash) and the consumer group of counting workers needs to scale horizontally to keep up with bursts tens of times above average rate.
- The Count-Min Sketch's **width and depth** are a direct memory-versus-accuracy trade-off; under-sizing it during a viral spike increases collision-driven overestimation right when accuracy matters most, so sizing has to account for expected peak cardinality per bucket, not just average.
- Summing sketches across many buckets to answer a window query gets more expensive as window size grows; for very large windows, periodically pre-merging older buckets into coarser, less granular summary sketches keeps the per-query sum bounded.
- A single event stream partitioned naively by hashtag can create a hot partition when one topic goes extremely viral; partitioning strategy may need to account for this skew rather than assuming uniform distribution across hashtags.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Reaching for an exact hash map or SQL GROUP BY count query== as the counting mechanism, without recognizing that unbounded hashtag cardinality makes that memory usage unbounded over time.
- ⚠️ ==Trying to implement a perfectly continuous sliding window with per-event expiration==, instead of the much cheaper discrete-bucket approximation that real systems use.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that a Count-Min Sketch cannot enumerate its contents, and designing a 'top N' feature as if querying the sketch directly would produce a ranked list.
- ⚠️ Ranking purely by raw mention count and being surprised the trending list never changes, missing that spike/velocity relative to a baseline is what actually captures 'trending' as a concept.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a Count-Min Sketch only overestimate counts and never underestimate them, and why does that matter for this use case?**

> **Model Answer:** Each hashtag is hashed by several independent functions into a shared array of counters, so two different hashtags can **collide** into the same counter and inflate each other's apparent count, but a counter can never be decremented below what real increments put into it, so an estimate (the minimum across all of a hashtag's hashed positions) can only be too high, never too low. For trending, this means a topic might rarely and briefly get bumped up by collision noise, but it will never be hidden or undercounted, which is the safer failure mode for a discovery feature.

**Q: How would you size the Count-Min Sketch's width and depth for a live event where mention volume for one topic can spike 20x?**

> **Model Answer:** **Width** controls collision probability, more counters per row means fewer distinct hashtags collide into the same slot, and **depth** (number of hash functions/rows) controls how many independent chances there are to avoid all collisions for a given item, since the estimate takes the minimum across rows. Sizing has to target the peak expected cardinality and count magnitude per bucket, not the average, since undersizing during exactly the highest-value moment (a breaking event) is when inflated counts would do the most damage to ranking quality.
