- `bucket_id (e.g. minute-aligned timestamp)`
- `sketch (a fixed-size Count-Min Sketch: an array of counter rows, one per hash function)`
*Notes:* One compact sketch per fixed time bucket (e.g. 1-minute buckets). The sliding window's count for a hashtag is the **sum of its estimated count** across all buckets currently inside the window; the oldest bucket is dropped as a new one is added, approximating a continuously sliding window with discrete steps.

### Entity: `heavy_hitters`
- `hashtag (indexed)`
- `window_id`
- `estimated_count`
*Notes:* A small, explicitly tracked candidate set (a **heap or top-K structure**) of hashtags likely to be trending, maintained alongside the sketch so the system doesn't need to enumerate every distinct hashtag ever seen to answer 'what's in the top 10 right now.'

### Entity: `topic_metadata`
- `hashtag (unique)`
- `first_seen_at`
- `category (nullable, e.g. sports, politics, entertainment)`
*Notes:* Lightweight metadata for display purposes only, not part of the counting hot path.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Why use a Count-Min Sketch instead of an exact hash map of hashtag to count?
A Count-Min Sketch is a fixed-size 2D array of counters plus several independent hash functions. To increment a hashtag's count, it's hashed by each function and the corresponding counter in each row is incremented. To estimate a count, the same hashes are looked up and the **minimum across rows** is returned (minimum, because hash collisions can only inflate a counter, never deflate it, so the smallest observed value is the closest to truth).

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Exact hash map: perfectly accurate counts, but memory ==grows linearly== with the number of distinct hashtags ever seen, which is unbounded and, at real scale, includes huge amounts of spam and one-off noise
- Count-Min Sketch: fixed memory regardless of cardinality, and counts are guaranteed to only ever overestimate, never underestimate, but rare hashtags can occasionally get inflated counts from collisions, and there is no way to enumerate 'all hashtags' from the sketch alone, only to query counts for a known hashtag
- The practical answer, used here, combines both: the sketch handles counting at fixed memory cost, while a separate small top-K heavy-hitters structure (updated alongside it) tracks the candidate set of likely-trending hashtags explicitly, since the sketch alone can't produce a top-N list, only answer 'how many for this specific hashtag'

### How do you approximate a continuously sliding time window using discrete buckets, and what error does that introduce?
A perfectly exact 'last 60 minutes, updated every second' window would require ==expiring individual mention events== the instant they age past exactly 60 minutes ago, which means tracking and later removing every individual event, defeating the whole point of using a compact sketch. Instead, time is divided into fixed buckets (e.g. 1-minute buckets), each with its own sketch, and the window's count is the sum across the last 60 buckets, with the oldest bucket dropped and a new one added every minute.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Continuously exact sliding window: no staleness at the boundary, but requires per-event expiration bookkeeping that is exactly the unbounded-memory problem this design is trying to avoid
- Fixed discrete buckets (e.g. 1-minute granularity): the window updates in visible steps rather than continuously, so a mention that just aged out of the oldest bucket disappears all at once rather than gradually, but this granularity is invisible to users looking at a trending list and makes the whole computation a cheap sum over a fixed number of small sketches
- Smaller buckets (e.g. 10 seconds) reduce the step-change granularity at the cost of more sketches to sum per query; the bucket size is a tunable trade-off between smoothness and per-query computation cost

### Raw mention count versus spike/velocity ranking: what actually counts as 'trending'?
Ranking purely by mention count in the window means the same perpetually popular topics (a huge fanbase's daily hashtag, for instance) dominate the trending list every single day, which isn't what users mean by 'trending', they mean **something unusual happening right now**.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Raw count ranking: simple, cheap, directly derived from the sketch sum, but surfaces the same evergreen topics repeatedly and rarely reflects breaking news
- Spike/velocity ranking (current window count versus a rolling baseline average for that same hashtag): surfaces genuine anomalies and breaking events, which is what users actually expect from a 'trending' feature, but requires maintaining a longer-running baseline per candidate hashtag, which is more storage and computation on top of the sketch
- A practical middle ground: use raw sketch counts to cheaply narrow down to a top-K candidate set per bucket, then only compute the more expensive baseline/velocity comparison for that small candidate set, not for every hashtag ever seen

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The mention ingest stream is the ==first pressure point== during a live event; it needs to be partitioned (e.g. by hashtag hash) and the consumer group of counting workers needs to scale horizontally to keep up with bursts tens of times above average rate.
- The Count-Min Sketch's **width and depth** are a direct memory-versus-accuracy trade-off; under-sizing it during a viral spike increases collision-driven overestimation right when accuracy matters most, so sizing has to account for expected peak cardinality per bucket, not just average.
- Summing sketches across many buckets to answer a window query gets more expensive as window size grows; for very large windows, periodically pre-merging older buckets into coarser, less granular summary sketches keeps the per-query sum bounded.
- A single event stream partitioned naively by hashtag can create a hot partition when one topic goes extremely viral; partitioning strategy may need to account for this skew rather than assuming uniform distribution across hashtags.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Reaching for an exact hash map or SQL GROUP BY count query== as the counting mechanism, without recognizing that unbounded hashtag cardinality makes that memory usage unbounded over time.
- ⚠️ ==Trying to implement a perfectly continuous sliding window with per-event expiration==, instead of the much cheaper discrete-bucket approximation that real systems use.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that a Count-Min Sketch cannot enumerate its contents, and designing a 'top N' feature as if querying the sketch directly would produce a ranked list.
- ⚠️ Ranking purely by raw mention count and being surprised the trending list never changes, missing that spike/velocity relative to a baseline is what actually captures 'trending' as a concept.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a Count-Min Sketch only overestimate counts and never underestimate them, and why does that matter for this use case?**

> **Model Answer:** Each hashtag is hashed by several independent functions into a shared array of counters, so two different hashtags can **collide** into the same counter and inflate each other's apparent count, but a counter can never be decremented below what real increments put into it, so an estimate (the minimum across all of a hashtag's hashed positions) can only be too high, never too low. For trending, this means a topic might rarely and briefly get bumped up by collision noise, but it will never be hidden or undercounted, which is the safer failure mode for a discovery feature.

**Q: How would you size the Count-Min Sketch's width and depth for a live event where mention volume for one topic can spike 20x?**

> **Model Answer:** **Width** controls collision probability, more counters per row means fewer distinct hashtags collide into the same slot, and **depth** (number of hash functions/rows) controls how many independent chances there are to avoid all collisions for a given item, since the estimate takes the minimum across rows. Sizing has to target the peak expected cardinality and count magnitude per bucket, not the average, since undersizing during exactly the highest-value moment (a breaking event) is when inflated counts would do the most damage to ranking quality.

# Design a Comment System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `YouTube • Reddit • Disqus` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The comment tree itself is easy to store, the hard part is that '**nested and paginated**' are in tension: any query that returns a natural-looking thread has to fetch a **bounded slice** of a tree of unbounded depth and width ==without ever materializing the whole thing==, while simultaneously deciding what counts as spam fast enough to not slow down the very users who aren't spamming.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a comment system that can be embedded under any piece of content
(a video, an article, a post): users can post a top-level comment or reply
to an existing comment, forming nested threads, and can sort a thread by
top, newest, or most controversial. The system must resist spam under
heavy concurrent posting. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is there a hard cap on nesting depth, or can replies nest arbitrarily deep (reply to a reply to a reply, indefinitely)?
*Why it matters:* Unbounded depth makes both storage traversal and UI rendering harder (deeply nested threads become unreadable past a few levels anyway). Most real systems cap visual nesting at some depth and flatten deeper replies, which materially simplifies both the data model and the read query.

#### Q: What does 'controversial' sorting mean here, closest to a 50/50 upvote/downvote split, or highest total engagement with a low ratio?
*Why it matters:* This decides what has to be tracked per comment. A simple ratio-based definition only needs the existing upvote/downvote counts. A more nuanced definition (e.g. weighting by total vote volume so a 3-vote 50/50 comment doesn't outrank a 3,000-vote near-50/50 comment) needs a real scoring formula, not just a ratio.

#### Q: Does spam detection need to happen synchronously before a comment is visible, or can a comment appear immediately and get retroactively removed if flagged as spam?
*Why it matters:* Synchronous spam scoring adds latency to every single comment post, including the vast majority that aren't spam. Asynchronous post-then-moderate keeps posting fast for everyone, at the cost of a spam comment being briefly visible before removal.

#### Q: Roughly how deep and wide can a single popular thread get, are we talking dozens of comments or hundreds of thousands?
*Why it matters:* At dozens of comments, a naive 'fetch everything for this post' query is fine. At hundreds of thousands, on a single viral video for instance, pagination and lazy-loading of nested replies stop being a nice-to-have and become the core design constraint.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can post a top-level comment on a piece of content, or reply to any existing comment.
- A user can view a comment thread sorted by top, newest, or controversial.
- Replies nest under their parent comment and are loaded on demand as a user expands a thread.
- The system rate-limits and flags likely spam without blocking normal commenting activity.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Posting a comment must feel instant, well under a second, to keep the commenting experience fluid even under load.**
- **Reading the first page of a popular thread must be fast regardless of how many total comments that thread eventually accumulates.**
- **The system must tolerate a small number of extremely large threads (hundreds of thousands of comments on one popular piece of content) without degrading performance for the much more common small threads.**
- **Spam and abuse controls must not meaningfully increase posting latency for the vast majority of legitimate users.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 100 million daily active users across all embedding sites/apps
- 8% of daily active users post at least one comment per day, averaging 1.5 comments each
- Each comment view (a user opening a thread) loads on average 30 comments across pagination and lazy-expanded replies
- 1 in 500 posted comments is spam or abusive content that gets flagged

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Comments posted per day:** 100,000,000 * 0.08 * 1.5 = 12 million comments/day ≈ 139 writes/sec average
- **Comment reads per day:** Assume each of the 8 million commenting users also opens roughly 4 threads a day to read (not post): 8,000,000 * 4 = 32 million thread opens/day, each pulling ~30 comments ≈ 960 million comment reads/day ≈ 11,111 reads/sec average
- **Spam comments flagged per day:** 12,000,000 / 500 = 24,000 spam comments/day ≈ 0.28/sec average, low volume but must not slow down the other 99.8%
- **Peak comments on a single viral thread:** A single trending video can draw 500,000+ comments over its lifetime; loading even the first page of that thread must not depend on its total size, otherwise the biggest threads become the slowest to load

*Capacity Takeaway:* Comment posting itself is **low volume** (under 150 writes/sec on average), so the driving constraint isn't write throughput, it's that comment count per thread varies from a handful to hundreds of thousands, and any read query has to perform identically regardless of that variance, which is a **pagination and indexing problem**, ==not a scaling-writes problem==.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A write path: a user posts a comment, the app server first checks a
cheap, synchronous rate-limit counter (per user, short window); if within
limits, the comment is written immediately with status visible, the
parent's reply_count is incremented, and the comment is enqueued for
asynchronous, heavier spam scoring. A spam-scoring path: workers pull
queued comments, compute a spam score from signals like posting rate, link
density, and text similarity to other recent comments, and flip status to
removed or pending_review if the score crosses a threshold, all without
having delayed the original post. A read path: fetching a thread means
fetching a page of top-level comments ordered by the requested sort
(indexed range scan), and separately, on demand, fetching a page of any
given comment's direct replies only when a user expands it, so a thread
with hundreds of thousands of comments still renders its visible portion
in constant time.

    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    app["App Servers"]:::server
    ratelimit["Rate Limit Cache"]:::cache
    commentsdb[("Comments Store")]:::db
    queue>"Spam Scoring Queue"]:::queue
    worker["Spam Scoring Workers"]:::server
    readcache["Thread Page Cache"]:::cache

    lb --> app
    app -->|"check rate limit"| ratelimit
    app -->|"write comment (visible)"| commentsdb
    app -.->|"enqueue spam scoring"| queue
    queue -.-> worker
    worker -.->|"flip status if spam"| commentsdb
    commentsdb -.->|"populate sorted page"| readcache
    app -->|"read thread page"| readcache
```

#### Posting a comment and expanding a reply thread

#### Controversial score needs vote volume, not just ratio

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/content/{contentId}/comments` | Body: { text, parent_comment_id? }. Creates a top-level comment or a reply if parent_comment_id is given. |
| `GET` | `/api/content/{contentId}/comments?sort=top|new|controversial&cursor=` | Returns a paginated page of top-level comments for the content, sorted as requested. |
| `GET` | `/api/comments/{commentId}/replies?cursor=` | Returns a paginated page of direct replies to a given comment, loaded on demand as a thread is expanded. |
| `POST` | `/api/comments/{commentId}/vote` | Body: { direction: up | down | none }. Casts, changes, or removes a vote on a comment, feeding top and controversial sorting. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `comments`
- `comment_id (time-sortable)`
- `content_id (indexed, the video/post/article this thread belongs to)`
- `parent_comment_id (nullable, null means top-level)`
- `author_id, text`
- `upvotes, downvotes`
- `reply_count (denormalized)`
- `status (visible, pending_review, removed)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Indexed on (content_id, parent_comment_id, sort_key) so fetching a page of top-level comments or a page of a specific comment's replies is a bounded range scan, never a full-tree traversal.

### Entity: `spam_signals`
- `comment_id`
- `score (0 to 1, likelihood of spam)`
- `signals (rate, link density, text similarity to recent comments, account age)`
*Notes:* Computed asynchronously after a comment is accepted and shown; a score above a threshold flips the comment's status to pending_review or removed without having blocked the original post.

### Entity: `rate_limit_counters`
- `user_id (or IP, for anonymous posting if allowed)`
- `window (e.g. current 1-minute bucket)`
- `count`
*Notes:* A short-lived, fast counter (e.g. in Redis with a TTL) checked synchronously before accepting a post, this is the cheap, fast-path spam control that runs on every comment; the heavier async scoring is the second layer.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you paginate a tree so a massive thread doesn't have to be loaded to show its first screen?
A comment tree can be arbitrarily wide (many top-level comments) and arbitrarily deep (replies to replies). Returning a whole thread as one nested JSON blob means the response size scales with total thread size, which is exactly backwards, the most popular content should not have the slowest comment section.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Materialize the full nested tree per request: simplest to implement and easy for a client to render in one pass, but response size and query cost scale with total comment count, making the most-commented content the slowest to load
- Paginate top-level comments and lazily fetch replies per branch only when expanded: every request is bounded regardless of total thread size, but the client needs multiple round trips to fully explore a thread, and a comment's reply_count needs to be denormalized and shown so users know there's more to expand
- The lazy, per-branch approach is what every real large-scale comment system uses, since it's the only one whose cost doesn't grow with the platform's own success

### Top, newest, and controversial: what does each sort actually require, and why is controversial the hardest?
Newest is a straightforward sort on created_at. Top is a straightforward sort on a vote-based score (like net upvotes, or a time-decayed score similar to a hot ranking). Controversial has to capture 'closely split opinion' rather than just 'high engagement,' which needs a formula that considers both the ratio of up to down votes and the total volume, not either alone.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Controversial as pure upvote/downvote ratio closest to 50/50: cheap to compute, but a comment with 1 upvote and 1 downvote scores as maximally controversial, which is clearly not the intent, it needs meaningful volume to actually be controversial
- Controversial weighted by total vote volume (e.g. a score that only rewards a near-even split once vote count crosses some minimum threshold): better matches intuition, but requires a slightly more involved scoring formula recomputed periodically, similar to how a hot ranking works
- In practice, controversial is computed the same way as a hot/top score: periodically recalculated per comment from its (upvotes, downvotes) pair and stored, not recalculated live per read, since the read path should stay a cheap indexed sort regardless of the scoring formula's complexity

### Should spam detection block the post, or let it through and moderate afterward?
A comment could be held pending until a spam classifier scores it, or accepted immediately and re-evaluated in the background. The first guarantees no visible spam ever appears, but ties posting latency to the classifier's speed for every single comment. The second keeps posting instant for the overwhelming majority of legitimate users, at the cost of spam being briefly visible.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous pre-post spam scoring: no spam is ever visible even briefly, but every legitimate comment now waits on classifier latency, and a classifier outage becomes a posting outage for everyone
- Asynchronous post-then-moderate: posting stays fast and available even if the classifier is slow or degraded, and spam is caught and removed within seconds typically, at the cost of a short visibility window for spam
- A hybrid used in practice: a cheap, fast synchronous check (rate limits, obvious blocklist patterns) blocks the clearest cases immediately, while a heavier async model handles subtler spam after the fact, balancing latency against how much spam visibility is tolerable

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A small number of extremely large threads (a viral video's comment section) dominate read load; the lazy per-branch pagination approach is what keeps these from degrading the read path for everyone else, but the underlying index still needs to handle range scans over hundreds of thousands of rows for a single content_id efficiently.
- reply_count as a denormalized counter on the parent comment needs the same batched-update treatment as a vote counter under high concurrent reply volume on one popular comment, to avoid row-lock contention.
- The spam-scoring queue needs to keep up during coordinated spam bursts (bot floods), and should shed load gracefully, e.g. deprioritizing scoring for low-risk-looking users, rather than let a burst delay scoring for everyone.
- Sort-order indexes (top, controversial) need periodic recomputation as votes accumulate; for very active threads this recomputation job itself needs to be incremental (updating only recently-voted comments) rather than rescoring an entire large thread on every run.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Returning an entire nested comment tree== in one response, which makes the platform's most popular content also its slowest to load.
- ⚠️ Implementing spam detection as a **synchronous blocking step** for every comment, adding latency for the 99%+ of legitimate posts to catch the rare spam ones.
- ⚠️ Defining 'controversial' as a raw vote ratio ==without a volume threshold==, which ranks a single 1-up-1-down comment as more controversial than a heavily debated one with thousands of votes.
- ⚠️ Forgetting to denormalize **reply_count** on the parent comment, forcing an expensive count query every time a thread is rendered.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is pagination of nested replies harder than pagination of a flat list like a news feed?**

> **Model Answer:** A flat feed paginates along a single dimension, time or rank, and a cursor unambiguously says 'give me the next N after this point.' A comment tree has two dimensions: breadth (how many top-level comments, and how many replies each has) and depth (how many levels deep). Naively paginating breadth-first still risks loading massive numbers of replies for one heavily-discussed comment, which is why replies are fetched lazily per branch, on demand, rather than eagerly included in the parent thread's page.

**Q: Why put spam scoring after the comment is already visible instead of before?**

> **Model Answer:** Because spam is rare (roughly 1 in 500 comments in this estimate) but the classifier work isn't free, and tying every single comment's posting latency to that classifier means 499 legitimate comments pay a latency cost to catch 1 spam comment. Accepting the comment immediately behind a fast, cheap synchronous rate-limit check, then scoring asynchronously and removing it within seconds if flagged, keeps the common case fast and only costs a brief visibility window on the rare case.

    app -->|"check rate limit"| ratelimit
    app -->|"write comment (visible)"| commentsdb
    app -.->|"enqueue spam scoring"| queue
    queue -.-> worker
    worker -.->|"flip status if spam"| commentsdb
    commentsdb -.->|"populate sorted page"| readcache
    app -->|"read thread page"| readcache
```

#### Posting a comment and expanding a reply thread

#### Controversial score needs vote volume, not just ratio

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/content/{contentId}/comments` | Body: { text, parent_comment_id? }. Creates a top-level comment or a reply if parent_comment_id is given. |
| `GET` | `/api/content/{contentId}/comments?sort=top|new|controversial&cursor=` | Returns a paginated page of top-level comments for the content, sorted as requested. |
| `GET` | `/api/comments/{commentId}/replies?cursor=` | Returns a paginated page of direct replies to a given comment, loaded on demand as a thread is expanded. |
| `POST` | `/api/comments/{commentId}/vote` | Body: { direction: up | down | none }. Casts, changes, or removes a vote on a comment, feeding top and controversial sorting. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `comments`
- `comment_id (time-sortable)`
- `content_id (indexed, the video/post/article this thread belongs to)`
- `parent_comment_id (nullable, null means top-level)`
- `author_id, text`
- `upvotes, downvotes`
- `reply_count (denormalized)`
- `status (visible, pending_review, removed)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Indexed on (content_id, parent_comment_id, sort_key) so fetching a page of top-level comments or a page of a specific comment's replies is a bounded range scan, never a full-tree traversal.

### Entity: `spam_signals`
- `comment_id`
- `score (0 to 1, likelihood of spam)`
- `signals (rate, link density, text similarity to recent comments, account age)`
*Notes:* Computed asynchronously after a comment is accepted and shown; a score above a threshold flips the comment's status to pending_review or removed without having blocked the original post.

### Entity: `rate_limit_counters`
- `user_id (or IP, for anonymous posting if allowed)`
- `window (e.g. current 1-minute bucket)`
- `count`
*Notes:* A short-lived, fast counter (e.g. in Redis with a TTL) checked synchronously before accepting a post, this is the cheap, fast-path spam control that runs on every comment; the heavier async scoring is the second layer.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you paginate a tree so a massive thread doesn't have to be loaded to show its first screen?
A comment tree can be arbitrarily wide (many top-level comments) and arbitrarily deep (replies to replies). Returning a whole thread as one nested JSON blob means the response size scales with total thread size, which is exactly backwards, the most popular content should not have the slowest comment section.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Materialize the full nested tree per request: simplest to implement and easy for a client to render in one pass, but response size and query cost scale with total comment count, making the most-commented content the slowest to load
- Paginate top-level comments and lazily fetch replies per branch only when expanded: every request is bounded regardless of total thread size, but the client needs multiple round trips to fully explore a thread, and a comment's reply_count needs to be denormalized and shown so users know there's more to expand
- The lazy, per-branch approach is what every real large-scale comment system uses, since it's the only one whose cost doesn't grow with the platform's own success

### Top, newest, and controversial: what does each sort actually require, and why is controversial the hardest?
Newest is a straightforward sort on created_at. Top is a straightforward sort on a vote-based score (like net upvotes, or a time-decayed score similar to a hot ranking). Controversial has to capture 'closely split opinion' rather than just 'high engagement,' which needs a formula that considers both the ratio of up to down votes and the total volume, not either alone.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Controversial as pure upvote/downvote ratio closest to 50/50: cheap to compute, but a comment with 1 upvote and 1 downvote scores as maximally controversial, which is clearly not the intent, it needs meaningful volume to actually be controversial
- Controversial weighted by total vote volume (e.g. a score that only rewards a near-even split once vote count crosses some minimum threshold): better matches intuition, but requires a slightly more involved scoring formula recomputed periodically, similar to how a hot ranking works
- In practice, controversial is computed the same way as a hot/top score: periodically recalculated per comment from its (upvotes, downvotes) pair and stored, not recalculated live per read, since the read path should stay a cheap indexed sort regardless of the scoring formula's complexity

### Should spam detection block the post, or let it through and moderate afterward?
A comment could be held pending until a spam classifier scores it, or accepted immediately and re-evaluated in the background. The first guarantees no visible spam ever appears, but ties posting latency to the classifier's speed for every single comment. The second keeps posting instant for the overwhelming majority of legitimate users, at the cost of spam being briefly visible.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous pre-post spam scoring: no spam is ever visible even briefly, but every legitimate comment now waits on classifier latency, and a classifier outage becomes a posting outage for everyone
- Asynchronous post-then-moderate: posting stays fast and available even if the classifier is slow or degraded, and spam is caught and removed within seconds typically, at the cost of a short visibility window for spam
- A hybrid used in practice: a cheap, fast synchronous check (rate limits, obvious blocklist patterns) blocks the clearest cases immediately, while a heavier async model handles subtler spam after the fact, balancing latency against how much spam visibility is tolerable

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A small number of extremely large threads (a viral video's comment section) dominate read load; the lazy per-branch pagination approach is what keeps these from degrading the read path for everyone else, but the underlying index still needs to handle range scans over hundreds of thousands of rows for a single content_id efficiently.
- reply_count as a denormalized counter on the parent comment needs the same batched-update treatment as a vote counter under high concurrent reply volume on one popular comment, to avoid row-lock contention.
- The spam-scoring queue needs to keep up during coordinated spam bursts (bot floods), and should shed load gracefully, e.g. deprioritizing scoring for low-risk-looking users, rather than let a burst delay scoring for everyone.
- Sort-order indexes (top, controversial) need periodic recomputation as votes accumulate; for very active threads this recomputation job itself needs to be incremental (updating only recently-voted comments) rather than rescoring an entire large thread on every run.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Returning an entire nested comment tree== in one response, which makes the platform's most popular content also its slowest to load.
- ⚠️ Implementing spam detection as a **synchronous blocking step** for every comment, adding latency for the 99%+ of legitimate posts to catch the rare spam ones.
- ⚠️ Defining 'controversial' as a raw vote ratio ==without a volume threshold==, which ranks a single 1-up-1-down comment as more controversial than a heavily debated one with thousands of votes.
- ⚠️ Forgetting to denormalize **reply_count** on the parent comment, forcing an expensive count query every time a thread is rendered.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is pagination of nested replies harder than pagination of a flat list like a news feed?**

> **Model Answer:** A flat feed paginates along a single dimension, time or rank, and a cursor unambiguously says 'give me the next N after this point.' A comment tree has two dimensions: breadth (how many top-level comments, and how many replies each has) and depth (how many levels deep). Naively paginating breadth-first still risks loading massive numbers of replies for one heavily-discussed comment, which is why replies are fetched lazily per branch, on demand, rather than eagerly included in the parent thread's page.

**Q: Why put spam scoring after the comment is already visible instead of before?**

> **Model Answer:** Because spam is rare (roughly 1 in 500 comments in this estimate) but the classifier work isn't free, and tying every single comment's posting latency to that classifier means 499 legitimate comments pay a latency cost to catch 1 spam comment. Accepting the comment immediately behind a fast, cheap synchronous rate-limit check, then scoring asynchronously and removing it within seconds if flagged, keeps the common case fast and only costs a brief visibility window on the rare case.

# Design a Follow/Follower Graph Service

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Twitter/X • Instagram` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This isn't really a database design problem, it's a **graph-partitioning** problem wearing a database costume: any single edge is trivial to store, but there is ==no way to shard billions of directed edges by user_id that keeps every hot query== (followers of X, followees of X, is-A-following-B, mutual follows of A and B) local to one shard at once, so the whole design is about which queries you make cheap and which ones you accept will fan out.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Forget the timeline for a moment. Design just the piece that answers "who
follows whom": a user can follow or unfollow another user, we can list a
user's followers and followees, check whether A follows B, and find mutual
follows between two users, all at a scale of billions of directed edges.
Design the service that owns this data.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the read pattern: mostly single-edge checks ('does A follow B', shown on every profile view), mostly listing followers/followees, or mostly mutual-follow / friend-of-friend queries?
*Why it matters:* A single-edge existence check is a point lookup that any sharding scheme handles well. Listing followers of a celebrity with 50 million followers, or computing 'friends in common,' are range and intersection queries that behave completely differently and push the design toward different storage engines.

#### Q: How skewed is the follower distribution, do we have celebrity accounts with tens of millions of followers, and regular accounts with a few hundred?
*Why it matters:* The same skew problem that breaks timeline fan-out shows up here: a celebrity's follower list is a single row's edge list with tens of millions of entries, which changes how you paginate, cache, and shard that one row's data compared to a normal account.

#### Q: Does this service need to serve strongly consistent reads (e.g. 'follow' must be immediately visible everywhere), or is a short eventual-consistency window acceptable?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether the graph store can be an eventually-consistent, horizontally-scaled key-value layer (cheap, fast) or needs stronger consistency guarantees (more expensive, more coordination), and it directly affects how other services like feed fan-out can safely consume this data.

#### Q: Do downstream systems (like the feed fan-out service) need to query this graph in bulk (e.g. 'give me all 50,000 followers of user X right now'), or only one edge at a time?
*Why it matters:* Bulk consumption by other services is exactly why this tends to become its own dedicated service in real companies rather than a table inside the main app database: it has a distinct, very hot, very specific access pattern that would otherwise compete with unrelated application traffic.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can follow another user (creates a directed edge) and unfollow (removes it).
- Given a user, list their followers (who follows them) and their followees (who they follow), both paginated.
- Check whether user A follows user B (a single boolean lookup).
- Given two users, return their mutual follows (the set of users both A and B follow), and support a basic 'people you may know' style friend-of-friend query.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **The is-following existence check must be extremely low latency (single-digit milliseconds), since it's rendered on every profile view and every tweet/post author line.**
- **The system must handle extreme skew: a normal account with 300 followers and a celebrity account with 50 million followers must both be servable without one degrading the other.**
- **The graph must scale to hundreds of billions of directed edges (well beyond one machine's memory or disk) while staying horizontally scalable by adding more shards.**
- **High availability for reads is more important than perfect real-time consistency; a follow that takes a second or two to be reflected everywhere is acceptable, a profile page that fails to load is not.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 million total user accounts
- Average followee count per user is 300, giving roughly 150 billion directed edges total
- A small number of celebrity accounts (roughly 10,000 of them) have between 1 million and 50 million followers each
- Each edge (follower_id, followee_id, created_at) is roughly 24 bytes of raw data, before index overhead
- Is-following checks happen on roughly 2 billion profile/post views per day

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total edges to store:** 500,000,000 users * 300 average followees ≈ 150 billion directed edges (each edge is stored, or indexed, in both directions, so effectively 300 billion index entries)
- **Raw storage for edges:** 150,000,000,000 edges * 24 bytes ≈ 3.6 TB of raw edge data, times roughly 2x for bidirectional indexing ≈ 7.2 TB, easily beyond a single machine and firmly in sharded-cluster territory
- **Is-following check QPS:** 2,000,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 23,000 checks/sec average, likely 5-10x that at peak, so design for ~150,000-200,000 QPS on this single lookup alone
- **Celebrity follower list size:** A single celebrity row can have 50,000,000 follower edges; listing or paginating that one user's followers is itself a 'big data' problem, not a normal row read

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that actually drives this design isn't total edge count, it's the **follower-list size skew**: one account's follower edge-list can be five orders of magnitude larger than another's, which means naive uniform sharding by user_id creates ==enormous hot shards==, and this graph service exists specifically to isolate that problem from the rest of the product.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A write (follow/unfollow) hits an app server, which writes the edge into
two denormalized tables in the same logical operation: follows_by_follower
(sharded by follower_id, answers "who do I follow") and follows_by_followee
(sharded by followee_id, answers "who follows me"), plus an async update to
a cached follower/following counter. Reads split by access pattern: an
is-following check is a single point lookup against follows_by_follower,
cacheable per (follower_id, followee_id) pair; a followers list is a
cursor-paginated range scan against follows_by_followee, which for
celebrity accounts is itself sharded further across multiple physical
partitions since one logical row can't fit on one physical shard; mutual
follows are computed by fetching both users' followee lists (capped and
cached for large accounts) and intersecting them, which is the one query
in this service that's inherently a fan-out/scatter-gather rather than a
point lookup.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Follow graph service: dual-write for both query directions

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    gateway["API Gateway"]:::server
    app["Graph App Servers"]:::server
    cache["Edge Cache"]:::cache
    byfollower[("follows_by_follower")]:::db
    byfollowee[("follows_by_followee")]:::db
    counters["Counter Store"]:::cache
    client --> gateway
    gateway --> app
    app -->|"is-following check"| cache
    cache -.->|"miss -> read"| byfollower
    app -->|"write edge"| byfollower
    app -->|"write edge (denormalized)"| byfollowee
    app -.->|"async increment"| counters
```

#### A follow action, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client calls POST /api/follows ({ followee_id })"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server writes edge into follows_by_follower (sharded by follower_id)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. App server writes edge into follows_by_followee (sharded by followee_id)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Async job increments follower/following counters (eventually consistent)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Invalidate is-following cache entry for this pair (so the next check reflects the new edge)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Follower count skew across accounts (power law)

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/follows` | Body: { followee_id }. The authenticated user follows followee_id, creates a directed edge. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/follows/{followeeId}` | The authenticated user unfollows followeeId, removes the directed edge. |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/followers` | Paginated list of userId's followers (cursor-based, not offset-based, since celebrity lists are enormous and shift constantly). |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/following` | Paginated list of accounts userId follows. |
| `GET` | `/api/follows/check` | Query params: follower_id, followee_id. Returns a boolean, the single hottest endpoint in the service. |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/mutual/{otherUserId}` | Returns the set of users both userId and otherUserId follow, used for 'X mutual friends' badges and friend-of-friend suggestions. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `follows_by_follower`
- `follower_id (partition key)`
- `followee_id (clustering key, sorted)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Optimized for 'who does X follow' (used heavily by fan-out and by the following-list page); sharded by follower_id, and since followee counts are relatively bounded per user, this table stays evenly distributed.

### Entity: `follows_by_followee`
- `followee_id (partition key)`
- `follower_id (clustering key, sorted)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* A deliberately denormalized second copy of the same edges, optimized for 'who follows X'; sharded by followee_id, and this is the table that gets skewed, since celebrity rows here are enormous compared to everyone else's.

### Entity: `follow_counts`
- `user_id (key)`
- `follower_count (approximate counter)`
- `following_count (approximate counter)`
*Notes:* A cached, eventually-consistent counter, updated asynchronously, so displaying '50.2M followers' on a profile never requires a full row scan/count of the edge table.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you shard a graph where the two natural query directions want opposite partition keys?
Sharding by follower_id makes 'who do I follow' a single-shard query, since one user's followee list lives entirely on one shard. But that same choice scatters 'who follows X' across every shard, since X's followers are spread across whichever shard each of their followers happens to live on. The reverse is true if you shard by followee_id instead. There is no single sharding key that makes both directions cheap.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Shard only by follower_id: 'who do I follow' is fast and local, but 'who follows me' requires querying every shard and merging results, unusable at this scale for a feature every profile page needs
- Shard only by followee_id: the reverse problem, 'who follows me' is fast, 'who do I follow' becomes a scatter-gather
- The actual answer: store the edge twice, once in each direction, in two separately sharded tables (follows_by_follower and follows_by_followee). This roughly doubles write cost and storage, but turns both hot read directions into single-shard lookups, which is worth the trade given how much more frequent reads are than writes.

### How do you handle a celebrity's follower list, which is too large for one shard's normal row?
Even after sharding follows_by_followee by followee_id, a single followee_id (a celebrity) can have 50 million follower rows, which is a 'wide row' that overwhelms a normal shard's capacity and creates a hot spot, since every read/write for that one user hammers a single physical shard while other shards sit idle.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Leave wide rows as-is: simplest, but creates severe hot-spotting, one shard does dramatically more work than its neighbors purely because it happens to host a celebrity
- Sub-shard (bucket) any followee whose follower count crosses a threshold, splitting their follower list across multiple physical partitions by a secondary hash, and merge results at read time: solves the hot-spot problem, but adds real complexity, every read against a bucketed user now needs a fan-out across its own buckets instead of a single lookup
- In practice, systems detect celebrity-scale rows dynamically and only pay the bucketing complexity cost for the small number of accounts that actually need it, keeping the common case (a normal user's follower list) simple

### Mutual follows and friend-of-friend suggestions: intersecting two potentially huge sets
Computing mutual follows means intersecting user A's followee set with user B's followee set. For two normal users this is trivial (a few hundred items each). For a normal user and a celebrity, intersecting against 50 million followees isn't something you want to do live on every profile view.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Compute the intersection live at query time: always correct and fresh, cheap for two normal-sized accounts, but prohibitively expensive when one side of the intersection is celebrity-scale
- Precompute and cache mutual-follow counts/samples for common pairings (e.g. cache 'mutuals with your own followees' since that's the actual product surface, not arbitrary user pairs), accepting slight staleness in exchange for a bounded, cheap read
- Cap the working set: only ever compute against the first N (say 5,000) most-recent or most-relevant followees of the larger account rather than the full set, trading perfect completeness for a bounded, predictable query cost, which is what most products actually ship since exact completeness rarely matters for a 'mutual friends' badge

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Celebrity rows remain the sharpest edge case in this system just like in feed fan-out; dynamic sub-sharding of wide rows is necessary once a followee's follower count crosses a threshold, or a small number of accounts will dominate cluster load.
- The is-following check, despite being the simplest query in the system, is also by far the highest-QPS one (rendered on nearly every post and profile); it needs an aggressive, short-TTL cache in front of the graph store, since it's read far more often than the underlying edge changes.
- Follower/following counts must never be computed with a live COUNT over the edge table at this scale; they need to be maintained as async, eventually-consistent counters updated on every follow/unfollow.
- As a dedicated service consumed heavily by the feed fan-out pipeline, this service's availability becomes a dependency for the entire product; it needs its own scaling, monitoring, and failure isolation (e.g. serving slightly stale cached data during an outage) rather than sharing fate with the main application database.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Modeling follows as a single table with one sharding key and assuming both directions of lookup will be equally fast, when in reality one direction will always end up doing a cluster-wide scatter-gather.
- ⚠️ Treating every followee_id row as roughly the same size, then being surprised when a handful of celebrity accounts create massive hot shards that dominate cluster load.
- ⚠️ Computing follower counts with a live count query against the edge table instead of maintaining a cached, asynchronously updated counter.
- ⚠️ Designing mutual-follows/friend-of-friend queries as an unbounded live set intersection, without capping the working set, so the query silently becomes unusably slow the moment either user has celebrity-scale followee counts.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does this service store every follow relationship twice, in two different tables?**

> **Model Answer:** Because 'who do I follow' and 'who follows me' are both extremely hot read paths that want opposite sharding keys to stay fast (follower_id for the first, followee_id for the second), and there is no single partitioning scheme that keeps both queries local to one shard. Storing the edge in two denormalized tables, one sharded each way, roughly doubles write cost but turns both directions into cheap, single-shard lookups, which is the right trade since reads vastly outnumber writes.

**Q: How would you serve the follower list of an account with 50 million followers without it overwhelming a single shard?**

> **Model Answer:** Detect when a followee's follower count crosses a threshold and sub-shard (bucket) that specific row's follower list across multiple physical partitions by a secondary hash, instead of letting it live on one shard. Reads against that user's follower list then fan out across its own buckets and merge, paying extra complexity only for the small number of accounts that actually need it, while normal users keep the simple single-shard path.

- Each edge (follower_id, followee_id, created_at) is roughly 24 bytes of raw data, before index overhead
- Is-following checks happen on roughly 2 billion profile/post views per day

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total edges to store:** 500,000,000 users * 300 average followees ≈ 150 billion directed edges (each edge is stored, or indexed, in both directions, so effectively 300 billion index entries)
- **Raw storage for edges:** 150,000,000,000 edges * 24 bytes ≈ 3.6 TB of raw edge data, times roughly 2x for bidirectional indexing ≈ 7.2 TB, easily beyond a single machine and firmly in sharded-cluster territory
- **Is-following check QPS:** 2,000,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 23,000 checks/sec average, likely 5-10x that at peak, so design for ~150,000-200,000 QPS on this single lookup alone
- **Celebrity follower list size:** A single celebrity row can have 50,000,000 follower edges; listing or paginating that one user's followers is itself a 'big data' problem, not a normal row read

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that actually drives this design isn't total edge count, it's the **follower-list size skew**: one account's follower edge-list can be five orders of magnitude larger than another's, which means naive uniform sharding by user_id creates ==enormous hot shards==, and this graph service exists specifically to isolate that problem from the rest of the product.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A write (follow/unfollow) hits an app server, which writes the edge into
two denormalized tables in the same logical operation: follows_by_follower
(sharded by follower_id, answers "who do I follow") and follows_by_followee
(sharded by followee_id, answers "who follows me"), plus an async update to
a cached follower/following counter. Reads split by access pattern: an
is-following check is a single point lookup against follows_by_follower,
cacheable per (follower_id, followee_id) pair; a followers list is a
cursor-paginated range scan against follows_by_followee, which for
celebrity accounts is itself sharded further across multiple physical
partitions since one logical row can't fit on one physical shard; mutual
follows are computed by fetching both users' followee lists (capped and
cached for large accounts) and intersecting them, which is the one query
in this service that's inherently a fan-out/scatter-gather rather than a
point lookup.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Follow graph service: dual-write for both query directions

```mermaid

    gateway["API Gateway"]:::server
    app["Graph App Servers"]:::server

    byfollower[("follows_by_follower")]:::db
    byfollowee[("follows_by_followee")]:::db

    gateway --> app

```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/follows` | Body: { followee_id }. The authenticated user follows followee_id, creates a directed edge. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/follows/{followeeId}` | The authenticated user unfollows followeeId, removes the directed edge. |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/followers` | Paginated list of userId's followers (cursor-based, not offset-based, since celebrity lists are enormous and shift constantly). |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/following` | Paginated list of accounts userId follows. |
| `GET` | `/api/follows/check` | Query params: follower_id, followee_id. Returns a boolean, the single hottest endpoint in the service. |
| `GET` | `/api/users/{userId}/mutual/{otherUserId}` | Returns the set of users both userId and otherUserId follow, used for 'X mutual friends' badges and friend-of-friend suggestions. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `follows_by_follower`
- `follower_id (partition key)`
- `followee_id (clustering key, sorted)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Optimized for 'who does X follow' (used heavily by fan-out and by the following-list page); sharded by follower_id, and since followee counts are relatively bounded per user, this table stays evenly distributed.

### Entity: `follows_by_followee`
- `followee_id (partition key)`
- `follower_id (clustering key, sorted)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* A deliberately denormalized second copy of the same edges, optimized for 'who follows X'; sharded by followee_id, and this is the table that gets skewed, since celebrity rows here are enormous compared to everyone else's.

### Entity: `follow_counts`
- `user_id (key)`
- `follower_count (approximate counter)`
- `following_count (approximate counter)`
*Notes:* A cached, eventually-consistent counter, updated asynchronously, so displaying '50.2M followers' on a profile never requires a full row scan/count of the edge table.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you shard a graph where the two natural query directions want opposite partition keys?
Sharding by follower_id makes 'who do I follow' a single-shard query, since one user's followee list lives entirely on one shard. But that same choice scatters 'who follows X' across every shard, since X's followers are spread across whichever shard each of their followers happens to live on. The reverse is true if you shard by followee_id instead. There is no single sharding key that makes both directions cheap.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Shard only by follower_id: 'who do I follow' is fast and local, but 'who follows me' requires querying every shard and merging results, unusable at this scale for a feature every profile page needs
- Shard only by followee_id: the reverse problem, 'who follows me' is fast, 'who do I follow' becomes a scatter-gather
- The actual answer: store the edge twice, once in each direction, in two separately sharded tables (follows_by_follower and follows_by_followee). This roughly doubles write cost and storage, but turns both hot read directions into single-shard lookups, which is worth the trade given how much more frequent reads are than writes.

### How do you handle a celebrity's follower list, which is too large for one shard's normal row?
Even after sharding follows_by_followee by followee_id, a single followee_id (a celebrity) can have 50 million follower rows, which is a 'wide row' that overwhelms a normal shard's capacity and creates a hot spot, since every read/write for that one user hammers a single physical shard while other shards sit idle.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Leave wide rows as-is: simplest, but creates severe hot-spotting, one shard does dramatically more work than its neighbors purely because it happens to host a celebrity
- Sub-shard (bucket) any followee whose follower count crosses a threshold, splitting their follower list across multiple physical partitions by a secondary hash, and merge results at read time: solves the hot-spot problem, but adds real complexity, every read against a bucketed user now needs a fan-out across its own buckets instead of a single lookup
- In practice, systems detect celebrity-scale rows dynamically and only pay the bucketing complexity cost for the small number of accounts that actually need it, keeping the common case (a normal user's follower list) simple

### Mutual follows and friend-of-friend suggestions: intersecting two potentially huge sets
Computing mutual follows means intersecting user A's followee set with user B's followee set. For two normal users this is trivial (a few hundred items each). For a normal user and a celebrity, intersecting against 50 million followees isn't something you want to do live on every profile view.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Compute the intersection live at query time: always correct and fresh, cheap for two normal-sized accounts, but prohibitively expensive when one side of the intersection is celebrity-scale
- Precompute and cache mutual-follow counts/samples for common pairings (e.g. cache 'mutuals with your own followees' since that's the actual product surface, not arbitrary user pairs), accepting slight staleness in exchange for a bounded, cheap read
- Cap the working set: only ever compute against the first N (say 5,000) most-recent or most-relevant followees of the larger account rather than the full set, trading perfect completeness for a bounded, predictable query cost, which is what most products actually ship since exact completeness rarely matters for a 'mutual friends' badge

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Celebrity rows remain the sharpest edge case in this system just like in feed fan-out; dynamic sub-sharding of wide rows is necessary once a followee's follower count crosses a threshold, or a small number of accounts will dominate cluster load.
- The is-following check, despite being the simplest query in the system, is also by far the highest-QPS one (rendered on nearly every post and profile); it needs an aggressive, short-TTL cache in front of the graph store, since it's read far more often than the underlying edge changes.
- Follower/following counts must never be computed with a live COUNT over the edge table at this scale; they need to be maintained as async, eventually-consistent counters updated on every follow/unfollow.
- As a dedicated service consumed heavily by the feed fan-out pipeline, this service's availability becomes a dependency for the entire product; it needs its own scaling, monitoring, and failure isolation (e.g. serving slightly stale cached data during an outage) rather than sharing fate with the main application database.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Modeling follows as a single table with one sharding key and assuming both directions of lookup will be equally fast, when in reality one direction will always end up doing a cluster-wide scatter-gather.
- ⚠️ Treating every followee_id row as roughly the same size, then being surprised when a handful of celebrity accounts create massive hot shards that dominate cluster load.
- ⚠️ Computing follower counts with a live count query against the edge table instead of maintaining a cached, asynchronously updated counter.
- ⚠️ Designing mutual-follows/friend-of-friend queries as an unbounded live set intersection, without capping the working set, so the query silently becomes unusably slow the moment either user has celebrity-scale followee counts.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does this service store every follow relationship twice, in two different tables?**

> **Model Answer:** Because 'who do I follow' and 'who follows me' are both extremely hot read paths that want opposite sharding keys to stay fast (follower_id for the first, followee_id for the second), and there is no single partitioning scheme that keeps both queries local to one shard. Storing the edge in two denormalized tables, one sharded each way, roughly doubles write cost but turns both directions into cheap, single-shard lookups, which is the right trade since reads vastly outnumber writes.

**Q: How would you serve the follower list of an account with 50 million followers without it overwhelming a single shard?**

> **Model Answer:** Detect when a followee's follower count crosses a threshold and sub-shard (bucket) that specific row's follower list across multiple physical partitions by a secondary hash, instead of letting it live on one shard. Reads against that user's follower list then fan out across its own buckets and merge, paying extra complexity only for the small number of accounts that actually need it, while normal users keep the simple single-shard path.

callout.title: Core Architectural Principle
callout.text: This isn't really a database design problem, it's a **graph-partitioning** problem wearing a database costume: any single edge is trivial to store, but there is ==no way to shard billions of directed edges by user_id that keeps every hot query== (followers of X, followees of X, is-A-following-B, mutual follows of A and B) local to one shard at once, so the whole design is about which queries you make cheap and which ones you accept will fan out.
